non-metals-compounds.detailed:
15. Non-metals and Their Compounds

JAMB syllabus focus: Important non-metals include hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine, sulphur and carbon. Their compounds have major industrial and biological importance. Hydrogen is used in ammonia production and as a fuel in some applications. Oxygen supports respiration and combustion. Nitrogen is used in ammonia manufacture, while ammonia is important in fertilizer production. Nitric acid is a strong acid and oxidizing agent used industrially. Chlorine is used in water treatment and manufacture of chemicals, although its safe handling is essential. Sulphur forms sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide, important in sulphuric acid manufacture; sulphur dioxide is also an air pollutant. Carbon forms carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and a vast range of organic compounds. Knowledge of preparation, properties, uses and environmental effects is central to this topic.

metals-compounds.name: Metals and Their Compounds
metals-compounds.detailed:
16. Metals and Their Compounds

JAMB syllabus focus: Metals generally conduct heat and electricity, are malleable and ductile, and form positive ions. Their reactivity varies and can be arranged in a reactivity series. Very reactive metals such as potassium and sodium are extracted by electrolysis, while less reactive metals may be obtained by reduction of their ores. Iron is extracted from haematite in the blast furnace using coke, limestone and hot air. Aluminium is extracted from purified alumina by electrolysis in molten cryolite. Copper, zinc and other metals have important uses, and transition metals often form coloured compounds and show variable oxidation states. Corrosion is the deterioration of metals through chemical or electrochemical reactions; iron rusting requires oxygen and water. Protection includes painting, coating, alloying and sacrificial protection.

organic-compounds.name: Organic Compounds
organic-compounds.detailed:
17. Organic Compounds

JAMB syllabus focus: Organic chemistry concerns carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives. Carbon forms four covalent bonds and can produce chains, branches and rings. Homologous series have the same functional group and general formula, with successive members differing by CH2. Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons; alkenes and alkynes contain carbon-carbon multiple bonds. Important reactions include combustion, substitution, addition, oxidation, cracking and polymerization. Functional groups determine the characteristic chemistry of alcohols, carboxylic acids, esters and other compounds. Isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different arrangements. Polymers are large molecules formed from repeating monomer units and may be addition or condensation polymers.

chemistry-and-industry.name: Chemistry and Industry
chemistry-and-industry.detailed:
18. Chemistry and Industry

JAMB syllabus focus: Industrial chemistry applies chemical principles to manufacture useful products on a large scale. Important Nigerian and global industries include petroleum refining, petrochemicals, fertilizer manufacture, cement production, glass, soap and detergent production, paints and food processing. Industrial processes require attention to raw materials, reaction conditions, catalysts, energy use, yield, separation, safety and waste control. The Haber process produces ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen under appropriate pressure, temperature and catalyst conditions. The Contact process produces sulphuric acid through oxidation of sulphur dioxide and subsequent absorption steps. Petroleum is separated by fractional distillation into fractions with different boiling ranges. Industrial chemistry connects laboratory reactions with economic production and environmental responsibility.

measurement-and-units.name: Measurement and Units
measurement-and-units.notes:
Measurement and Units

Measurement is the comparison of a physical quantity with an agreed standard. Physics uses SI base quantities such as length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity. Derived quantities are formed from base quantities; for example velocity is length divided by time and force is mass multiplied by acceleration. Measurements should include a numerical value and unit. Accuracy concerns closeness to the true value, while precision concerns the consistency of repeated measurements. Errors may be systematic or random. Dimensional analysis is useful for checking equations and converting units.

Core ideas

  • Understand definitions and physical meaning.
  • Know the SI units and standard relationships.
  • Apply the principle to numerical and conceptual questions.
  • Check units, signs, directions and limiting conditions.

JAMB focus

Expect questions that combine definitions, interpretation of diagrams or graphs, formula selection and short calculations. Always identify the known quantities before selecting an equation.

Common errors

  • Using the wrong unit or prefix.
  • Ignoring direction for vector quantities.
  • Substituting inconsistent units.
  • Using a formula outside its stated conditions.

Apply the principles to JAMB-style objective questions.

scalars-and-vectors.name: Scalars and Vectors
scalars-and-vectors.notes:
Scalars and Vectors

A scalar has magnitude only, while a vector has both magnitude and direction. Distance, speed, mass, time and energy are scalars. Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum are vectors. Vectors can be represented by directed line segments and resolved into perpendicular components. For perpendicular components, the magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of the components. Vector addition follows the triangle or parallelogram rule.

Core ideas

  • Understand definitions and physical meaning.
  • Know the SI units and standard relationships.
  • Apply the principle to numerical and conceptual questions.
  • Check units, signs, directions and limiting conditions.

JAMB focus

Expect questions that combine definitions, interpretation of diagrams or graphs, formula selection and short calculations. Always identify the known quantities before selecting an equation.

Common errors

  • Using the wrong unit or prefix.
  • Ignoring direction for vector quantities.
  • Substituting inconsistent units.
  • Using a formula outside its stated conditions.

motion.name: Motion
motion.notes:
Motion

Motion is the change of position with time relative to a reference point. Distance is the total path length and displacement is the directed change from initial to final position. Uniform motion has constant velocity; non-uniform motion involves changing velocity. Position-time and velocity-time graphs provide information about motion. The slope of a displacement-time graph gives velocity, while the slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration and the area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.

speed-velocity-and-acceleration.name: Speed, Velocity and Acceleration
speed-velocity-and-acceleration.notes:
Speed, Velocity and Acceleration

Speed is distance per unit time and velocity is displacement per unit time. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. For constant acceleration, v=u+at, s=ut+1/2 at² and v²=u²+2as. Negative acceleration is often called deceleration. Average speed is total distance divided by total time; it is not generally the arithmetic mean of two speeds unless the time intervals are equal.

projectile-motion.name: Projectile Motion
projectile-motion.notes:
Projectile Motion

A projectile is an object moving under gravity after being launched, with air resistance neglected. Its horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontal velocity remains constant while vertical velocity changes at acceleration g. For initial speed u at angle θ, horizontal component is u cosθ and vertical component is u sinθ. On level ground, range R=u²sin2θ/g, time of flight T=2u sinθ/g and maximum height H=u²sin²θ/(2g).

  • Know the SI units and standard relationships.
  • Apply the principle to numerical and conceptual questions.
  • Check units, signs, directions and limiting conditions.

newtons-laws.name: Newton's Laws of Motion
newtons-laws.notes:
Newton's Laws of Motion

Newton's first law states that a body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted upon by a resultant external force. The second law relates resultant force to rate of change of momentum; for constant mass F=ma. The third law states that forces occur in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies. Free-body diagrams help identify forces such as weight, normal reaction, tension, friction and thrust.

  • Know the SI units and standard relationships.
  • Apply the principle to numerical and conceptual questions.
  • Check units, signs, directions and limiting conditions.

Work is done when a force causes displacement in its direction. W=Fs cosθ. Kinetic energy is 1/2mv² and gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is mgh. Power is the rate of doing work, P=W/t, and for a force acting along velocity P=Fv. Conservation of energy states that energy is not created or destroyed but transformed between forms. Efficiency is useful output energy divided by input energy multiplied by 100 percent.

machines.name: Machines
machines.notes:
Machines

Machines make work easier by changing the size or direction of a force. Mechanical advantage is load divided by effort, while velocity ratio is distance moved by effort divided by distance moved by load. Efficiency is MA/VR multiplied by 100 percent. momentum-and-collisions.name: Momentum and Collisions
momentum-and-collisions.notes:
Momentum and Collisions

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p=mv. It is a vector quantity. In an isolated system, total momentum remains constant. Impulse equals change in momentum and is also force multiplied by time. In elastic collisions, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. In inelastic collisions, momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not fully conserved. Recoil and explosions can be explained using conservation of momentum.

equilibrium-of-forces.name: Equilibrium of Forces
equilibrium-of-forces.notes:
Equilibrium of Forces

A body is in translational equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces is zero. For rotational equilibrium, the net moment about any point is also zero. elasticity.name: Elasticity

Elasticity

Elasticity is the ability of a material to regain its original shape after a deforming force is removed, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded. Young's modulus is stress divided by strain. Elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring is 1/2kx².

sound.name: Sound
sound.notes:
Sound

Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave requiring a material medium. Its speed depends on the medium and temperature. Frequency determines pitch, while amplitude is related to loudness. Echoes arise from reflection of sound. Resonance occurs when a system is driven near its natural frequency. Beats are produced when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies interfere.

heat-and-temperature.name: Heat and Temperature
heat-and-temperature.notes:
Heat and Temperature

Temperature indicates the degree of hotness and is related to average molecular kinetic energy. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Specific latent heat is energy required per unit mass for a change of state without temperature change, Q=mL.

gas-laws.name: Gas Laws
gas-laws.notes:
Gas Laws

For a fixed mass of gas, Boyle's law states that pressure is inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature, PV=constant. The ideal gas equation is PV=nRT.

Series circuits have the same current through components; parallel branches have the same potential difference.

modern-physics.notes:
Modern Physics

Modern physics includes atomic, nuclear and quantum ideas. Electromagnetic radiation can behave as particles called photons with energy E=hf. Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random; alpha, beta and gamma radiations have different penetrating and ionising powers.
